title: Nightcap: candidate annotated mismatch log - runtime infra
content:
TL;DR: strong systems intuition on scheduler/batching but notable mismatch between stated tradeoffs and concrete designs. Behavioral signals positive (team fit, product curiosity). Technical depth uneven: excellent latency reasoning; weaker on KV-cache lifecycle and graceful-fallback integration. Recommend follow-up take-home focused on a live rollout plan + end-to-end failure scenarios before moving to hiring panel.

Candidate: Jonah Park — background: 6y infra (2x startups), last role runtime engineer at small LLM infra shop. Applied for Senior Runtime Engineer (IC3/4 depending on scope). Interviewers: me (Iris), Maya (serving runtime), Galen (platform infra).

High-level impression:
- Confident explainer, draws diagrams quickly, comfortable with latency/throughput numbers.
- Uses real metrics language (p50/p90/p99, tokens/sec) which is good signal.
- Tendency to default to sync flow when async/circuit-breaker would be better (flag).
- Pragmatic but occasionally hand-wavy on edge conditions (race around cache eviction, warmup).

Key positives (what I'd want on team):
- Batching/scheduler mental model: described an adaptive-batch algorithm that adjusted window by p90 latency, batching threshold, and per-customer priority. Could sketch pseudo-code and complexity. Good.
- Latency SLO thinking: prioritized tail latency over average for user-facing routes, advocated smaller batches + prefix caching for low-latency flows.
- Cost awareness: suggested quantization + per-route model routing for cost/quality tradeoffs. Referenced quantization library experience (but no deep math).
- Communication: explains tradeoffs clearly, asked clarifying Qs, good at asking for constraints early.

Signals of concern / mismatches (main reason for this doc):
1) KV cache lifecycle: when pressed on long-lived KV shards, they proposed an in-memory LRU per-GPU and a periodic checkpoint to S3. But when probed on eviction semantics (concurrent reads/writes + cache-coherence), they defaulted to "we can just lock it" — no discussion of lock contention, sharding strategies, or lock-free designs.
   - Why it worries me: Redwood's autoscaling/multi-tenant patterns require more nuanced approaches (per-model shards, fine-grained seq-level eviction, per-worker durable checkpoints). Jonah's answers were plausible but not concrete.
2) Graceful fallback and rollout policies: suggested fallback to smaller model under capacity pressure. But didn't describe how to preserve user session continuity (KV transfer, prompt stitching, hallucination regressions).
   - Follow-up ask: give me an end-to-end plan for a canary that fails over to a quantized variant while preserving conversation state. I want concrete steps and rollback criteria.
3) Race conditions in cold-start: admitted to relying on synchronous cold-start path for certain model variants (blocking requests) with retry/backoff. No clear mitigation for thundering herd if autoscale is slow.
   - Good candidate would propose pre-warming heuristics, predictive scaling signals (enqueue metrics), or temporary queuing with degraded tokens-per-second fallback. Jonah mentioned these in passing but lacked a detailed mechanism.

Raw snippets (notes-to-self verbatim):
- "we'd shard KV by model + user prefix, keep hot prefixes in memory, write cold to object store" (ok but how to atomically move between hot/cold?)
- "locks are fine if contention low" (too hand-wavey)
- "canary should be ephemeral and routed via a header" (good, but what about traceability and rollback metrics?)

Behavioral notes:
- Teamwork: liked the "pair on-call" idea for cross-team ops, offered examples where they ran postmortems and ownership handoffs.
- Curiosity: asked about product roadmap (Redwood Dedicated autoscale), shows product empathy.
- Pressure handling: stayed calm under iterative pushback on KV designs.

Recommendation (what I want next):
- Do a short, time-boxed take-home: design a canary rollout that routes 5% traffic to a quantized model variant with KV cache migration and rollback triggers. Deliverable: 1–2 page plan + sequence diagram + 6 test cases for regressions. Timebox: 4–6 hours.
- If take-home is satisfactory, proceed to panel for final culture + matching expectations.

Interview scoring (raw):
- System design: 6/10 (good on batching/scheduling, weak on KV lifecycle and coherence)
- Operational maturity: 5/10 (postmortem examples ok, but design lacked failure-mode specifics)
- Communication: 8/10
- Overall hire? Low-leaning on strong yes; leaning toward conditional hire if take-home shows improved rigor.

Unresolved questions / follow-ups for panel:
- Has candidate shipped a rollout that involved migrating in-memory state between model versions? (ask for exact example/PR link)
- What concrete metrics did they rely on to trigger autoscale vs queue? (which signals, what thresholds)
- How familiar with kernel-level GPU memory tuning (OOM patterns, torch-backed allocator)? They claimed experience but didn't demonstrate deep troubleshooting steps.

Action items (personal):
- Send take-home prompt + example rubric to candidate (I will adapt the Canary Rollout doc from Confluence).
- Ask Maya to probe quantization tradeoff questions in next panel (she has the ref tests).
- Add Jira task: follow-up-interview-jonah (assign to Maya), link to JIRA-INF-1427.

Quick note on candidate fit placement: could be strong match for a team focused on routing/scheduling/latency-first features (smaller blast radius), but less so for teams that require heavy on-node-state migration (Dedicated/private).

Notes to self: keep the take-home tight — force them to show how they'd preserve session KV across model variants. That will reveal whether the earlier hand-wavy parts were surface-level or an actual gap.

End.
